questions.prompt: Which command creates a new, empty Git repository in the current directory?
options: git init
git new
git create
git start
questions.explanation: git init creates the .git directory that stores repository data.

questions.prompt: Which command stages changes for the next commit?
options: git stage-all
git push
git add
git save
questions.explanation: git add copies changes into the index (staging area).

questions.prompt: Which command records the staged changes as a new commit?
options: git save
git commit
git record
git write
questions.explanation: git commit creates a commit from the contents of the index.

questions.prompt: Which command shows which files are modified, staged or untracked?
options: git log
git show
git diff --names
git status
questions.explanation: git status summarizes the state of the working tree and index.

questions.prompt: Which command copies an existing remote repository to your machine?
options: git clone
git copy
git fetch --all
git download
questions.explanation: git clone creates a local copy including history and sets up the origin remote.

questions.prompt: Which file tells Git which files or patterns to leave untracked?
options: .gitkeep
.gitconfig
.gitignore
.gitattributes
questions.explanation: .gitignore lists patterns of files that Git should not track.

questions.prompt: Which command creates a new branch called feature and switches to it?
options: git branch -d feature
git checkout -b feature
git merge feature
git switch feature --delete
questions.explanation: checkout -b (or git switch -c) creates and checks out the branch in one step.

questions.prompt: What does git pull do by default?
options: Fetches from the remote and merges into the current branch
Only downloads remote changes without touching your branch
Pushes local commits and then fetches
Deletes local commits that are not on the remote
questions.explanation: git pull is git fetch followed by git merge (or rebase if configured).

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of git stash?
options: Temporarily shelve uncommitted changes so you can work on a clean tree
Permanently delete uncommitted changes
Squash recent commits into one
Create a tag for the current commit
questions.explanation: git stash saves modified tracked files and staged changes so they can be re-applied later with git stash pop.

questions.prompt: How does git revert differ from git reset?
options: Revert deletes the commit from history entirely
Revert adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one, leaving history intact
Revert only works on uncommitted changes
Revert moves the branch pointer backwards
questions.explanation: Revert is safe for shared branches because it does not rewrite history; reset moves the branch pointer.

questions.prompt: What does git merge --no-ff do?
options: Aborts the merge if there are conflicts
Skips merge commits and rebases instead
Always creates a merge commit, even when a fast-forward is possible
Merges only files that have no conflicts
questions.explanation: --no-ff preserves the fact that a feature branch existed by recording an explicit merge commit.

questions.prompt: What does git cherry-pick <commit> do?
options: Moves the commit to the remote repository
Deletes the commit from its original branch
Merges the entire branch containing the commit
Applies the changes introduced by that commit as a new commit on the current branch
questions.explanation: Cherry-pick replays a single commit's changes onto HEAD, producing a new commit with a different hash.

questions.prompt: What does git reset --soft HEAD~1 do?
options: Moves the branch back one commit but keeps the changes staged
Moves the branch back one commit and discards all changes
Creates a new commit that reverses the last one
Unstages files without moving the branch
questions.explanation: --soft only moves HEAD/branch; the index and working tree stay as they were, so the changes remain staged.

questions.prompt: What does git diff --staged show?
options: The differences between the working tree and the index
The differences between two branches
The differences between the index and the last commit
The list of untracked files
questions.explanation: --staged (or --cached) compares the staging area against HEAD, i.e. what would be committed.

questions.prompt: You ran git reset --hard and lost commits. Which command helps you find and recover them?
options: git log --all --merges
git reflog
git stash list
git fsck --lost-found
questions.explanation: The reflog records where HEAD and branch tips have pointed, so you can find the old commit hash and reset or branch to it.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid rebasing commits that have already been pushed to a shared branch?
options: Rebase refuses to work on pushed commits
Rebase permanently deletes the remote branch
Rebase converts the commits into merge commits
Rebase rewrites those commits with new hashes, forcing collaborators to reconcile diverged history
questions.explanation: Rebased commits are new objects; anyone who based work on the old ones ends up with duplicated or conflicting history.

questions.prompt: In an interactive rebase, what does the "fixup" command do?
options: Melds the commit into the previous one and discards its message
Splits the commit into several smaller commits
Rewords the commit message only
Drops the commit and its changes
questions.explanation: fixup is like squash but keeps only the earlier commit's message.

questions.prompt: When can git merge perform a fast-forward?
options: When both branches changed different files
When the branches have no common ancestor
When the current branch tip is an ancestor of the branch being merged
When the other branch contains only one commit
questions.explanation: If there is no divergence, Git just moves the branch pointer forward and creates no merge commit.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of git push --force-with-lease over --force?
options: It pushes faster by skipping object checks
It refuses to overwrite the remote branch if it changed since you last fetched
It also rewrites remote tags
It merges remote changes automatically before pushing
questions.explanation: The lease check prevents you from clobbering commits that someone else pushed in the meantime.

questions.prompt: After git merge --squash feature followed by git commit, what is true of the resulting commit?
options: It has two parents like a regular merge commit
It is created automatically without a commit command
It has a single parent and does not record the feature branch commits as ancestors
It rewrites the feature branch commits with new hashes
questions.explanation: --squash stages the combined changes but does not create a merge relationship, so Git does not know the branch was merged.

questions.prompt: You make commits while in a detached HEAD state, then check out a branch. What happens to those commits?
options: They become unreachable and may eventually be garbage collected unless you create a branch or tag for them
They are automatically merged into the branch you check out
They are pushed to the remote as a new branch
They are permanently deleted immediately
questions.explanation: Commits only reachable from a detached HEAD are not on any branch; the reflog keeps them for a while, then gc may prune them.
